claims.text: Pre-exposure Q235 steel has a native oxide film.
The stability of the native oxide film governs the corrosion resistance of pre-exposure Q235 steel in harsh environments.
At room temperature, the native oxide film remains stable.
At room temperature, the native oxide film protects Q235 steel by limiting corrosive penetration.
Exposure to elevated temperatures below 100°C induces a phase or microstructural transformation in the native oxide film.
The temperature-induced oxide transformation makes the film less continuous and less protective.
Loss of oxide-film continuity and protectiveness increases corrosive attack on Q235 steel.
Elevated-temperature exposure in a chloride-rich, high-humidity environment will cause greater mass loss than room-temperature exposure.
Elevated-temperature exposure will produce deeper pitting than room-temperature exposure.
Elevated-temperature exposure will measurably change the phase composition of the native oxide film relative to room-temperature exposure.
Elevated-temperature exposure will measurably change the continuity of the native oxide film relative to room-temperature exposure.
In a benign, low-chloride and low-humidity environment, the native oxide film on untreated Q235 steel remains protective.
The proposed mechanism applies at moderate chloride concentrations, high humidity, and temperatures below 100°C.
The proposed mechanism may not apply under extreme chemical aggression or outside the stated temperature range.
